findings.consequence: Malformed reports lacking any time field are counted as valid and returned with 200. That is looser than the previous contract, and it contradicts the stated either/or rule between the two specs.
findings.explanation: The old BrowserReport dataclass required `timestamp`. The new serializer makes both `age` and `timestamp` optional. The validators only reject the case where both are present, and they only run when their field is supplied. A report with neither field, such as `{"body":{},"type":"crash","url":"https://a.com","user_agent":"x","destination":"default","attempts":1}`, now passes validation. The docstrings say that exactly one must be present. Also, `initial_data.get("age")` is truthy-based, so `age: 0` together with `timestamp: 5` is accepted.
findings.title: Serializer accepts reports with neither age nor timestamp

findings.consequence: Every POST to the preprod artifact assemble endpoint fails with an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500). This includes requests from orgs without the feature flag, since the call comes before the flag check. The endpoint is unusable.
findings.explanation: `ProjectPreprodArtifactAssembleEndpoint.post` calls `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` before the feature-flag check. `Analytics.record` looks the event type up with `event_manager.get(...)`, which is `self._event_types[type]` and raises `KeyError` if the type is unregistered. The event is registered only as a side effect of importing `src/sentry/preprod/analytics.py`. A grep found no importer of that module: not the endpoint, not `sentry.analytics.events/__init__`, not `sentry.preprod.tasks`. `Analytics.setup` imports only `sentry.analytics.events`. The event class is therefore never registered at runtime.
findings.title: Preprod analytics event is never registered; assemble endpoint raises KeyError on every request

findings.consequence: When some errors are cached and others are not, or when an error is missing from nodestore or listed twice, the replay summary sent to Seer contains errors with the wrong details, and some errors are lost. The AI summary is then built from incorrect data.
findings.explanation: fetch_error_details builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, then pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` using zip. `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id, not a list aligned with the input. It deduplicates the ids. Its cache-miss path (nodestore/base.py:199-205) puts the items fetched from the service first and the cached items last. It may also leave out ids that have no data. So `events.values()` can be shorter than `error_ids`, in a different order, or both. The zip then gives an event's title, message and timestamp to the wrong `id`. If an id is missing, every later error shifts onto the wrong id.
findings.title: Error IDs are zipped with nodestore results by position, which misattributes or drops errors

findings.consequence: Users can no longer see which kind of grouping variant they are looking at, or read the tooltip explaining it. Any test that asserts on the 'Type' row would also fail.
findings.explanation: getVariantData used to push a 'Type' row, with an explanatory tooltip, for COMPONENT, CUSTOM_FINGERPRINT, BUILT_IN_FINGERPRINT, SALTED_COMPONENT and PERFORMANCE_PROBLEM variants. The change deletes all of these pushes. renderTitle only shows the description and contribution state, and nothing else in the file shows variant.type, so the information is no longer displayed anywhere in this component.
findings.title: Variant 'Type' row removed from grouping info for all variant types

findings.consequence: For any organization with the flag on, every table widget on a dashboard shows no columns and no rows, even though the query returned data. The flag is gated, so only flagged organizations are affected.
findings.explanation: In tableResultComponent, when the organization has the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature, the code renders TableWidgetVisualization with hard-coded placeholder props (columns={[]}, tableData with data: [] and empty meta). It ignores result.data, result.meta and the widget fields that the else branch passes to StyledSimpleTableChart. The loading state and the custom field renderers are dropped as well.
findings.title: Table widget renders an empty table when 'use-table-widget-visualization' is enabled

findings.consequence: The tabs and the vitals are no longer vertically centered when their heights differ. The three right-hand loading placeholders lose their spacing and alignment. This is a minor visual regression.
findings.explanation: The removed Container extended FlexBox, so the main row had display:flex, align-items:center, gap:space(1) and justify-content:space-between. The replacement `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` sets only justify, so align-items and gap are lost. In Placeholder, the right-hand `<Flex>` (line 27) also lost the align-items:center and gap that the old FlexBox gave it. The other migrated sites (integratedOrgSelector, outer Placeholder Flex) pass align and gap explicitly, so these two are inconsistent with them.
findings.title: Flex migration in traceTabsAndVitals drops align-items:center and gap from the old Container/FlexBox

findings.consequence: The partition's committed offset stops advancing at the gap. all_offsets grows without bound, and each commit pass rescans the range. After a restart, everything since the gap is reprocessed.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets walks range(start, max_offset+1) and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets (lines 89-93). Offsets never submitted to the tracker are not tracked. These include Kafka offset gaps from compaction or transaction markers, and any message that does not reach submit. Such an offset is treated as a hole, so the loop breaks there on every pass.
findings.title: Commit progress stalls permanently on any gap in offsets

findings.consequence: After a restart or rebalance, the last processed message of every partition is redelivered and processed again. For uptime results this means duplicate result processing.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets returns the highest fully processed offset (line 96), and _commit_loop passes that dict unchanged to commit_function. Arroyo/Kafka commit semantics expect the next offset to consume (processed offset + 1). Offset N, which has already been processed, is therefore committed as the resume position. mark_committed then records N as last_committed, so the tracker and Kafka agree on the same off-by-one value.
findings.title: Commits highest processed offset instead of next offset to consume

findings.consequence: After the first rebalance, every message routed to the thread-queue-parallel consumer is silently dropped and its offset is committed. The result is permanent loss of check-in results, with only 'Error submitting message to queue' logged.
findings.explanation: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__. create_thread_queue_parallel_worker passes that same pool to a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on every create_with_partitions call, which happens on every partition assignment or rebalance. Arroyo calls close() or terminate() on the old strategy when partitions are revoked. In queue_consumer.py, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(). That sets worker.shutdown and calls q.shutdown() on every queue, and the worker threads exit. The factory's queue_pool attribute stays non-None, because only ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() clears it. The next strategy therefore gets a dead pool. Its submit() calls work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches that in its generic `except Exception`, then does add_offset and complete_offset for the messa…
findings.title: Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by each strategy's close() and reused after a rebalance, so messages are committed without being processed

findings.consequence: The test doesn't verify the behaviour it claims to. If the consumer started committing past a failed message, or if it never committed anything, the test would give the same result either way. That hides a real regression in error and offset handling.
findings.explanation: The docstring of test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling (line 1876) says a processing error must not block offset commits for other messages. The test makes the first message (offset 100) raise and the second (offset 101) succeed. Line 1922 then asserts that no offset was committed for the partition, which is the opposite of the docstring. The assertion also passes if nothing is ever committed, so it can't tell the intended behaviour from a stalled consumer. I read only the test code. I did not check the consumer implementation.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and can't catch a regression

findings.consequence: The test fails, or passes only if the commit thread has not yet fired. It would not catch a regression where an error blocks commits, and it encodes the wrong expected behavior.
findings.explanation: The test's docstring says an error in processing must not block offset commits. The worker in queue_consumer.py (line 148-149) calls complete_offset in a `finally`, so a failed item 100 still completes. After item 101 succeeds, get_committable_offsets returns the partition, and the commit loop (about 1s interval) calls commit_function. The test still asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` at line 1922. That asserts the opposite of both the docstring and the code. The assertion fails once the commit loop runs. The test never checks that offset 101 was committed, so it does not verify the behavior it claims to.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting its docstring and the worker's behavior
